corrected_value.title: The Effects of Music in Advertising on Choice Behavior: A Classical Conditioning Approach

decisions.quote:
This paper focuses on replicating the first experiment in
Gerald Gorn’s article ‘‘The effects of music in advertising
on choice behavior: A classical conditioning approach,’’
published in the Journal of Marketing, 1982.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 0 identify the same tested original study: Gorn (1982), Experiment 1, published in Journal of Marketing, 46, 94. The conflicting_dois flag occurs only because the shipped row records the canonical Crossref/Sage publisher DOI (10.1177/002224298204600109) whereas the blind coding extracted the JSTOR DOI (10.2307/1251163) printed in the reference list (line 967). Prior replications discussed in the introduction are background context and not re-tested targets.

decisions.quote:
Aggregating our data, and excluding participants with
‘‘deviant’’ musical taste, we found no effect of music on
pen choice, N = 375; v2(1) = .00, p = .99, u = .00,
logOR = .00, 95% CI = .41 to .40. The 95% CI included
0, and did not include the original 2.17, nor the OR of
1.04 associated with a point null effect, nor the OR of
0.44 associated with Simonsohn’s (2013) u33% criterion
(for which our aggregated sample provides .57 power). In
unison, the three experiments failed to replicate the original
results.
decisions.reason: With the dependent original identity resolved to Gorn (1982), both shipped and blind codings agree on 'failed'. While Experiment 3 (updated music) showed a smaller significant effect driven by one experimental group, Experiments 1 and 2 were conclusive replication failures, and the authors state an explicit overall aggregate verdict across all three experiments ('In unison, the three experiments failed to replicate the original results'; 'in aggregate, our studies conclusively failed to replicate the original effect', p. 185), which governs under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1.

decisions.quote:
Three studies replicated a classroom experiment on single-exposure musical conditioning of consumer choice (Gorn, 1982), testing
whether simultaneous exposure to liked (vs. disliked) music and a pen image induced preferences for the shown (vs. a different) pen.
decisions.reason: With the dependent original identity resolved to Gorn (1982), both shipped and blind codings agree on 'replication'. The authors collected new experimental data across three independent student samples (N = 158, N = 190, and N = 91) to re-test Gorn's (1982, Experiment 1) musical conditioning finding.
